Junkyard Dog 1954 Dodge Royal Is a Derelict Hemi Mopar With Sad News All Over, Don't Look Underhood
32 photos
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante
Pretend you can go back in time – let’s say you have a dial phone that doubles as a time machine, and you turn back the wheels of chronology to the very early 1950s. There are no EVs, no plastic clothes, food is not yet fast (and it actually tastes like something you’d want to eat), and cars are on their way to beautiful masterpieces of automotive greatness. And then out of the sky, a marvelous invention lands on Planet Piston. The hemi V8 for cars.
When Chrysler Corporation introduced its revolutionary overhead-valve V8 architecture for the 1951 model year, American performance engineering changed forever. Known collectively as the first-generation hemi V8 family and produced until 1958, these powerplants featured hemispherical combustion chambers, crossflow cast-iron cylinder heads, dual rocker shafts, and centrally positioned spark plugs.
The war pushed Detroit in making quantum leaps in tech progress, and the aircraft industry didn’t stand pat. One of the side effects of having the gigantic auto industry shift its entire resources to war production is that innovations don’t stay on the frontlines once the conflict is over. Detroit openly admitted that WWII was a far greater incentive for new technologies than civilian competition could have ever been.
Among the many advancements made by the biggest car-making industry in the world, the hemispherical combustion chamber engine was deemed as a very suitable candidate for performance cars. Chrysler Corporation saw that the engine was good enough to make planes fly, so the idea of putting it in road cars was natural.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante The idea was far from new, but it had never before been adopted on a large scale. That aeronautical-inspired layout optimized airflow and flame travel, allowing Mopar engineers to extract extraordinary volumetric efficiency and durability from engines installed in regular production passenger cars.
Across their 8-year production run, the first-generation hemi engines spanned a dozen distinct variations because each corporate division engineered its own proprietary block casting and bore spacing. Chrysler inaugurated the design in 1951 under the FirePower moniker, producing three displacements over the decade.
The debut was with a 331-cubic-inch unit from 1951 to 1955, an enlarged 354-cubic-inch version for 1956, and the legendary 392-cubic-inch powerhouse that served during the 1957 and 1958 seasons. Those FirePower V8s propelled upscale Chrysler models including the Saratoga, New Yorker, Imperial, and the dominant 300-letter-series coupes from the 1955 C-300 through the 1958 300D.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante DeSoto joined the hemispherical ranks in 1952 with its FireDome V8, rolling out a handful of displacements through 1957: a 276, a 291, a 330, a 341, and finally a 345-cubic-inch dual-quad variant powering the DeSoto Firedome, Fireflite, and high-output Adventurer.
Dodge entered the Hemi arena in 1953 with its Red Ram V8, building four division-specific displacements through 1957: 241, 270, 315, and 325 cubic inches for Meadowbrook, Coronet, Royal, Custom Royal, and D-500 cars, while the 1957 D-501 borrowed Chrysler's 354-cubic-inch block. Plymouth never received a first-generation hemi, keeping flathead 6-cylinder engines until 1955, yet it redeemed that omission during the 426 Hemi era by becoming Mopar's best-selling Hemi division.
Notice that the early hemi motors weren’t particularly large in displacement – Dodge, for example, had the smallest hemi V8 ever fitted onto a Mopar product. 241 cubes is just under 4.0 liters, even under the first V8 that powered the iconic Mustang, the 260-incher of 1964-and-a-half.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Under the hood of a 1954 Dodge Royal sat the second-year 241.3-cubic-inch Red Ram Hemi V8, an oversquare design with a 3.4375-inch bore, a 3.250-inch stroke, five main bearings, and hydraulic lifters. While 1953 models and the 1954 Meadowbrook used 7.1:1 compression to make 140 horsepower, the 1954 Coronet and flagship Royal received a 7.5:1 compression ratio, delivering 150 horsepower at 4,400 rpm and 222 lb-ft of torque at 2,400 rpm.
It sounds impressive today – by coffee grinders’ standards – but that was the best money could buy in a low-price Doge back when Eisenhower was in the office. Breathing through a simpleton two-barrel Stromberg carburetor, the 241 hemi V8 earned high praise in period road tests conducted by Motor Trend and Mechanix Illustrated.
Depending on transmission choice, testers recorded 0 to 60 mph times between 12.3 and 16.2 seconds, quarter-mile runs of 18.8 to 20.3 seconds at 68 to 71 mph, and top speeds near 100 mph, while four-barrel Bonneville test cars captured 196 AAA stock records peaking at 108.36 mph.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante One surviving artifact from that early horsepower race recently surfaced on Steve Magnante’s YouTube channel, where the automotive historian documented a weathered 1954 Dodge Royal four-door sedan resting at R.P.J. Automotive in Hubbardston, Massachusetts.
Positioned above the Meadowbrook and Coronet trims, the top-tier Royal line came exclusively with V8 power and never offered a flathead 6-cylinder engine, with Dodge assembling 50,050 Royal more-door sedans during the 1954 run.
This disheartening sedan showcases the second year of Dodge's integrated envelope body shell, which replaced the protruding bolt-on rear fenders used in 1952. Subtle bolt-on chrome crown moldings atop the rear quarters hint at the imminent Forward Look era and its tailfin craze, while the tail panel pairs a round left-side fuel cap with a symmetrical right-side backup lamp, and license plate lights tucked inside the rear bumperettes.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Although decades of New England weather have dulled its finish, the sedan still wears its original two-tone paint, combining a white lower body with a Robin's Egg Blue roof and factory battleship gray coating across the inner trunk panels.
While spare doors and fenders rest inside the cabin, the Royal's front clip is gone because the yard owner sold the nose to restore a rare 1954 Dodge Coronet Indianapolis 500 Pace Car convertible. The remaining shell will likely be parted out further, as time has claimed the horsehair stuffing inside both bench seats, leaving only the bare steel coil springs that Chrysler engineers once tested for 100,000-mile durability.
Peering across the dashboard reveals an optional dash-mounted rearview mirror, a 120-mph speedometer, and a column shifter for Chrysler's cast-iron 2-speed PowerFlite automatic transmission. Down on the driver's floorboard sits a foot-operated plunger button that worked with a firewall vacuum diaphragm to squirt washer fluid onto the glass, beside a small trapdoor covering the inconvenient under-floor brake master cylinder that Chrysler relocated onto the firewall in 1955.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Although the 241-cubic-inch Red Ram Hemi V8 was removed years ago, the exposed frame still displays its independent front coil springs, rear leaf springs, power steering ram, and a mechanical 6-volt voltage regulator mounted on the firewall. Most remarkably, the underside of the hood preserves a factory sheet-metal air duct behind the slotted front Ram ornament, which channeled cool, dense ambient air straight into the oil-bath air cleaner atop the carburetor.
1954 also marked a drastic crunch for Detroit. Dodge was hit hard. In 1953, the division sold over 320,000 automobiles, the second-best year of the decade (after almost 342k vehicles produced in 1951). In ’54, sales dipped to 154,650 cars, the second from the bottom, sitting only above the dreadful 1958 Eisenhower Recession and its 138k Dodges.
The Royal line moved over 64,800 cars (most of them four-door sedans, with the two-door trio of hardtop, sedan, and convertible amassing some 14,800 combined). The Royal four-door was a sales champion, sitting together with its lesser sibling, the Coronet, at the top of the pyramid. Between them, the two four-door sedans mover over 100k units that year.

With up to 460 kW DC fast charging, the new BMW iX5 can add up to 170 miles in just 10 minutes. BMW proved it during a live public event for the first time.
BMW puts iX5 fast charging on display
BMW’s new electric vehicles are a step change from its previous-generation EVs. Based on its sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive system with 800V technology, the setup delivers up to a 30% increase in driving range and charging speeds compared to the Gen5 system.
In addition to new, highly efficient electric motors, the Gen6 eDrive uses new batteries with cylindrical cells that BMW says provide 20% greater energy density than the Gen5 prismatic cells.
To prove just how fast it can charge, BMW put the new iX5 50 xDrive to the test during an international media event in Southern California with IONNA and Alpitronic.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
During the event, the new iX5 hit a peak of 464 kW, even slightly higher than the 460 kW that BMW reported.
BMW said that with up to 460 kW peak charging, the iX5 60 xDrive can add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes. To charge the 144 kWh battery from 10% to 80% takes just 22 minutes.
BMW iX5 60 xDrive hits 464 kW (Source: BMW)
While the results are impressive, 460 kW is the peak rate, not the sustained rate during the entire charging session. Either way, it’s still impressive and quick enough to get you back on the road quickly.
Plus, the US does not have the hardware to support 460 kW charging. Alpitronic supplied the hardware, and the demo was at an IONNA charger.
BMW iX5 60 xDrive at an IONNA charger (Source: BMW)
BMW will launch the 2027 iX5 60 xDrive in the US in the first quarter of 2027, starting at $79,800. Official EPA figures are still pending, but BMW estimates the iX5 will offer up to 435 miles of range with a 144 kWh battery.
It’s powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, delivering a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque, which BMW says enables it to go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds.
The new iX5 is BMW’s first all-electric vehicle produced in the US. BMW is set to begin production at its Plant Spartanburg by the end of the year.

source_document.body:
CMB.Tech’s Mineral Europa, described by its Belgian shipowner as the world’s first ammonia-powered dry bulk carrier, has completed sea trials, marking a step toward commercial deployment of the alternative fuel in large ocean-going cargo ships.
The 210,000-deadweight-ton Newcastlemax was built at China’s Qingdao Beihai Shipyard and will operate under a charter agreement with Australian miner Fortescue. Its dual-fuel engine can run on ammonia or conventional marine fuel.
Following the trials, the vessel took on 1,000 metric tons of green ammonia in a ship-to-ship bunkering operation at Zhoushan, China. The Mineral Europa departed for Australia on its maiden voyage Oct. 14.
The vessel leads a broader fleet expansion. CMB.Tech (NYSE: CMBT ), based in Antwerp, plans deliveries of 21 ammonia-powered ships through 2029, comprising 18 dry bulk carriers, one containership and two chemical tankers. The company said Oct. 9 that most were expected to be delivered within the following nine months.
“Mineral Europa is the first of its kind, but many more will follow in the months and years ahead,” CMB.Tech Chief Executive Alexander Saverys said in the company’s announcement.
The business case for ammonia-powered shipping is decarbonization, not cheaper fuel, as ship owners are betting that long-term cargo contracts, lower emissions-related costs and protection against future regulation, particularly in Europe, will eventually outweigh more expensive ships and fuel. DNV’s assessment is that fuel cost remains the biggest barrier to making that equation work.
Ammonia-fueled newbuilds typically cost 15%–20% above conventional designs, according to maritime risk analyst DNV, and European green ammonia at about $2,900 per metric ton of marine-gas-oil-equivalent energy is roughly five times that of diesel fuel. Ammonia also requires nearly three times the fuel volume of diesel for equivalent energy, the analyst said, creating trade-offs among tank space, cargo capacity, range and bunkering frequency.
The Fortescue charter connects the new propulsion technology with a major dry bulk cargo customer. In June, the mining company agreed to charter up to 12 CMB.Tech Newcastlemax vessels. Up to three are to be delivered with dual-fuel ammonia engines, while the remainder are to be delivered ammonia-ready, according to reports.
CMB.Tech is also investing in the infrastructure needed to support ammonia-fueled operations, including fuel storage and bunker barges. The company said introducing the ships is only part of the transition, with safe and efficient fuel delivery also needed to support their deployment.
The owner is promoting green ammonia as a fuel produced using renewable electricity, water and air, and says ammonia releases no carbon dioxide when burned. That claim concerns combustion of the ammonia itself; Mineral Europa also retains the ability to operate on conventional marine fuel.
